title: Pity or courage
hookLine: by different means we reach the same end: sometimes mercy softens an enemy, sometimes courage (Essays 1.1)
carry: pity moves some hearts, courage moves others
last: AN IDLE MIND BOLTS; WATCH IT ON PAPER.

cards: Same fight, same parent, two different kids. One cries and says sorry, and the parent melts. The other stands there, chin up, and says, I did it, and I'd do it again, and somehow the parent melts for that one too.

Montaigne opens the whole book of Essays with this, in the very first chapter, though his examples are a good deal bloodier: a conqueror at the gates of a town, and the question of what makes him stop.

teach.b: First, the usual road. The title says it: by different means we arrive at the same end. When someone we've wronged has us in their power, Montaigne says, the common way to soften them is to give in and move them to pity.
Second, the other road. Sometimes the opposite works: courage and steadiness. His first story is a prince at the sack of a town.
The people, the women and the children, throw themselves at his feet, and he isn't moved.

Then he sees three gentlemen holding their ground against his whole army with astonishing boldness, and that is what stops his anger. He spares them, and then the town. Third, the surprise in the middle.

He'd be the one swayed by pity, he says, and more easily by pity than by admiration, though he knows the Stoics counted pity a fault. So the essay isn't a rule. It's two roads and two different hearts.
Fourth, the line that sends the whole book on its way.
Man, he writes, is a marvelously vain, varied, and wavering thing; it's hard to build any steady judgment on him. The essays after it keep trying to catch that wavering thing.
And it fits the week: a village content at home, true words without polish, the Tao's close, a tower, painted beams, a runaway horse.
Different roads into the same quiet work. Close to home, an approach that failed with one person might be the wrong road, not the wrong goal.

how: Some readers of Montaigne take the first chapter of the Essays as a key to the whole book: people are too varied for one rule, so the same end can be reached by opposite means.

o: different means, like pity or courage, can reach one end
choosing one firm rule and keeping it in every situation
leaving home to travel and see how other people live

games.q: Montaigne's first essay: tap the pairs.
p: give in and move them to pity
held their ground and stopped his anger

s: Montaigne says only pity can soften a conqueror
the essay's point is the opposite: by different means, pity or courage, we reach the same end.
Montaigne says he himself is more easily moved by pity
more by pity than by admiration, though he notes the Stoics counted pity a fault.
the prince in the story spared the town because the people begged
their pleas didn't move him; the courage of three gentlemen did.

games.q: you're the prince at the sack of the town. the people beg at your feet. then you see three men standing firm against your army. what moves you?
games.why: in Montaigne's story the pleas didn't move him, but the boldness of the three gentlemen stopped his anger, and he spared them and then the town.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you keep taking the same road and getting the same result: a conversation with a teenager, a habit you keep trying to quit, a coworker who won't budge.
Is your usual road soft or firm, talking or waiting? Picture the other road, just once, and see where it might go.

wordCard.voice: Different roads. Montaigne's first essay: by different means we reach the same end; sometimes pity softens a conqueror, sometimes courage does. Today's word.
